name: Seleucid Empire
summary: The largest Hellenistic kingdom formed from Alexander’s empire, founded by Seleucus I. It spread Greek culture from Syria to Iran until Rome annexed its last lands in 63 BCE.

location.value: Syria, Mesopotamia, Iran and at first Central Asia.

terrain.value: Mediterranean coast, the Tigris–Euphrates plain and the Iranian plateau.
terrain.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

climate.value: Mediterranean in the west, arid in the east.
climate.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

resources.value: The rich farmland of Mesopotamia and Syria, and trade routes to the east.
resources.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

disasters.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

urbanisation.value: Founded many Greek-style cities, including Antioch and Seleucia on the Tigris, among the largest cities of the age.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

disease.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

migration.value: Greek and Macedonian settlers moved to the new cities.
migration.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

economicBase.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

tradeRoutes.value: Routes linking the Mediterranean, India and Central Asia.
tradeRoutes.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

moneyAndTax.value: Silver tetradrachms with portraits of the kings; tribute from provinces.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

inequality.value: A Greek-Macedonian elite ruled over local peoples.
inequality.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

governmentType.value: Monarchy (basileus), with provinces (satrapies) inherited from Persia.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

keyRulers.value: Seleucus I (305–281 BCE), Antiochus I, Antiochus III the Great (223–187 BCE), Antiochus IV.

succession.value: Hereditary, but rival members of the royal family often fought.
succession.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

institutions.value: Satraps governed provinces; a Seleucid era calendar dated from 312 BCE.
institutions.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

stability.value: Frequent dynastic wars, especially in the 2nd century BCE.
stability.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

eliteConflict.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

armyAndTech.value: Macedonian phalanx, war elephants (from the Mauryas) and armoured cavalry.
armyAndTech.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

majorWars.value: Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE), Roman–Seleucid War and Magnesia (190 BCE), Maccabean Revolt (167–160 BCE).

territoryChange.value: About 3.9 million km² in 301 BCE, shrinking to Syria by about 100 BCE.
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Ptolemies, Rome, Parthia; a treaty with the Mauryas.
alliancesRivals.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

inventions.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

scienceEducation.value: Babylonian astronomy continued under Seleucid rule.
scienceEducation.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

openness.value: Greek culture spread among local elites.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

religion.value: Greek religion, Babylonian religion, Judaism and Zoroastrianism.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

artsArchitecture.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

socialStructure.value: Greek settlers, local elites and farmers.
socialStructure.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

sharedIdentity.value: Greek culture and loyalty to the Seleucid royal house.
sharedIdentity.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

neighbours.value: Ptolemaic Egypt, Rome, Parthia and the Mauryas.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

ideasReligions.value: Spread Hellenistic culture across western Asia.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

colonisation.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

riseSignals.value: Seleucus I took Babylon in 312 BCE.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

peakPeriod.value: Around 301 BCE, and again briefly under Antiochus III.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

declineSignals.value: Defeat at Magnesia (190 BCE) and losses to Parthia.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

outcome.value: Annexed by Rome under Pompey in 63 BCE.

sources.value: Greek historians, inscriptions, coins. Checked against Wikipedia (“Seleucid Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Good for major events; known mostly from Greek and Roman writers.

knownFor.label: War elephants
knownFor.note: Seleucus received 500 elephants from Chandragupta Maurya.

knownFor.label: Antioch
knownFor.note: One of the great cities of the ancient world.

knownFor.label: Tetradrachm coins
knownFor.note: Silver coins with portraits of kings.
